2026-11-20 · All platforms · Open-source software

This edition provides 84 complete documentation guides and 2 additional screened leads. 40 earlier screened entries received full guides. New and updated records carry their own dated evidence checks. Spatial-audio generation, film captions and camera-driven production illustrate different kinds of control. SAID maps detected sound events onto a panoramic view. Kdenlive’s subtitle workflow gives an editor text and timing inside an established non-linear editor. Other guides cover image-to-geometry handoffs, fabrication, lyric and notation drafts, and accessible media. Velo adds locally generated rehearsal textures to its live graph. ZigZag adds canvas-pinned feedback and version comparison for an AI-directed embroidery edit. Software licensing is reviewed independently of model terms, any paid service or required proprietary host. Documentation and published examples informed the quality checks. A metadata signal does not establish software eligibility. Unreviewed and excluded candidates remain in private research records. Live primary research captured 460 usable responses from 600 distinct URL attempts, including non-GitHub primary sources in 114 of 114 fields. 8 captures were size-bounded. The ecosystem notes record each configured source group. The notes identify limits such as access and rate restrictions, failed fetches and bounded discovery pages. The counts represent the documented searches and available pages. Evidence label counts were 0 Recommended, 1 Ready to try, 80 Quality unverified, 5 Experimental. The public Hugging Face Space at the checked revision, with the bundled examples and the released SAID PaSST checkpoint for noncommercial research. Search and review counts

114 creative fields; 1306/1306 repository queries attempted; 33/33 model-task queries attempted. 84758 distinct source candidates and 1432 model leads. 84 detailed profiles and 2 additional screened discoveries. Source gaps: 0 failed repository queries, 0 partial repository queries, 253 bounded repository queries, 0 failed model-task queries and 0 web ecosystem gaps. Raw search candidates include duplicates of known tools, excluded projects and projects awaiting review; they are not verified recommendations.

Profiles are based on current primary documentation. Creative quality and performance claims are attributed to the developers unless hands-on testing is explicitly recorded. Unknown hardware requirements stay unknown. Code, model weights, hosted services, and required proprietary hosts can have different terms.

Scope: Sketching a moving cue for a sound installation, VR scene or spatial Foley study.

  • Reproducible setup · documented: Use a Python 3.10 environment with a CUDA GPU and install the released package from source. Fetch the named diffusion and autoencoder checkpoints. T5-base downloads on first use. Independent reproduction has not been established in this review. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]
  • Maintenance and support · documented: The maintainer answered a licensing question on October 27 and added explicit source and model terms. Other platform support and independent maintenance checks remain open. [7]

Released checkpoints and the dataset carry CC BY-NC 4.0 restrictions. Direct waypoint input uses local inference. The optional natural-language parser calls a separate Gemini or OpenRouter service. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

This assessment is based on published sources. Hands-on verification remains pending. One source and a fixed short duration are the documented mode. A demo rendering leaves direction accuracy, listening quality and fit to a particular installation unverified.

How it uses AI

A physics-guided diffusion model generates a sound event along an authored trajectory and renders a first-order Ambisonics WAV. The user can supply the trajectory as waypoints. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

Introduction

PhysWave lets a sound designer describe one short sound and trace its movement around a listener. For a study, the provided waypoint files give direct control over movement without a hosted parser. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

What it is good for

Sketching a moving cue for a sound installation, VR scene or spatial Foley study. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

Demo & examples

The developers publish examples of stationary cues, an arc of typing and an approaching or receding sound. The documented output is about ten seconds of 16 kHz first-order Ambisonics. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

Install

Use a Python 3.10 environment with a CUDA GPU and install the released package from source. Fetch the named diffusion and autoencoder checkpoints. T5-base downloads on first use. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

  1. Obtain the official source or release linked below.
  2. Use a Python 3.10 environment with a CUDA GPU and install the released package from source. Fetch the named diffusion and autoencoder checkpoints. T5-base downloads on first use.
python -m physwave --condition examples/keyboard_arc.json --output outputs/keyboard.wav

First project

Start with a short, representative project and inspect the result before a larger batch. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

  1. Start from a supplied waypoint file and inspect its caption, times and angles.
  2. Change one movement parameter. Preserve the emitted JSON beside the WAV so another creator can trace the cue.
  3. Decode to the actual headphone or loudspeaker layout and check front/back direction and the apparent path.

Hardware & software

Requirements below are documented for this workflow. Unspecified limits are not inferred. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

Hardware
A CUDA GPU is required by the documented setup. Minimum VRAM, memory and storage remain undetermined.
Software
Python 3.10, CUDA-compatible runtime, both checkpoints and T5-base. A separate Ambisonics decoder is required for ordinary headphone monitoring.
Platforms
The maintainer documents a CUDA workflow. Equivalent native macOS or CPU-only inference remains undocumented in the reviewed setup.

License, model weights & costs

The full software license was reviewed. Model weights, assets and services remain separate. [2] [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

  • Weights: Apache-2.0 covers the project code and MIT covers the named Stable Audio Tools subset. Released checkpoints and the dataset carry CC BY-NC 4.0 restrictions.
  • Commercial: Software use follows Apache-2.0. Apache-2.0 covers the project code and MIT covers the named Stable Audio Tools subset. Released checkpoints and the dataset carry CC BY-NC 4.0 restrictions.
  • Cost: Direct waypoint input uses local inference. The optional natural-language parser calls a separate Gemini or OpenRouter service.

The fit of its maps to a new microphone arrangement is unresolved. The checkpoints carry a noncommercial research license. External hosting availability and quota apply.

How it uses AI

The project’s learned detector maps active sound events to labeled panoramic regions from spatial microphone recordings. Its CLI emits structured directional observations that can drive an authored visualization. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

Introduction

SAID places sound events on a panoramic map. The event and direction data can help an artist connect a sound field to a display or organize a multichannel recording. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

What it is good for

Prototyping an acoustic map for an installation or annotating events in a consented multichannel recording. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

Demo & examples

The maintainer provides four synchronized comparisons with published reference and predicted acoustic maps. The video pairs and benchmark are narrowly scoped to the recorded datasets and model variant. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

Install

Create an environment with Python 3.10–3.12, install the package from the source checkout and make FFmpeg available for visuals. The CLI retrieves the selected checkpoint on first run. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

  1. Obtain the official source or release linked below.
  2. Create an environment with Python 3.10–3.12, install the package from the source checkout and make FFmpeg available for visuals. The CLI retrieves the selected checkpoint on first run.
said demo --model said_passt

First project

Start with a short, representative project and inspect the result before a larger batch. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

  1. For the Ready to try scope, open the documented public demo and inspect a bundled recording first. Local or commercial operation requires its own evidence review.
  2. Inspect the packaged reference scenes and decide how labeled regions should enter the visual work.
  3. Validate microphone capsule order against the documented Eigenmike input before analyzing a new recording.
  4. Keep the DCASE JSON with the recording, channel map and model identification.

Hardware & software

Requirements below are documented for this workflow. Unspecified limits are not inferred. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

Input is specified for an Eigenmike signal or four selected capsules in the documented order. Minimum RAM, VRAM and disk space remain undocumented.
Software
Python 3.10–3.12, FFmpeg for demos, and the appropriate model artifact. DCASE JSON is the documented default inference output.
Platforms
The reviewed source describes a Python setup. Verified packaged builds and support on each operating system remain pending.

  • Commercial: Software use follows MIT. The project’s original software is MIT. Specified third-party components have their own grants. Published model checkpoints carry a noncommercial research license.

Included for the documented creative workflow. A complete guide and popularity do not establish output reliability. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6]

How it uses AI

WhisperX creates timestamped text from recordings and the pipeline aggregates transcripts and confidence information. Optional Azure OpenAI stages extract entities and summarize themes separately. [1] [3] [4]

Introduction

Ukuvula is an archival transcription workflow with separate metadata, speech, aggregation and enrichment stages. A collection editor can keep generated text tied to the recording and review it before publication. [1] [3] [4]

What it is good for

Building an initial text index and citation trail for a complex, rights-cleared set of oral recordings. [1] [3] [4]

Demo & examples

Install

Use the supplied conda environment with Python 3.10–3.11. Configure the metadata and media inputs for a single collection. Keep the optional cloud stages disabled when they are outside the collection’s permissions. [1] [3] [4]

  1. Obtain the official source or release linked below.
  2. Use the supplied conda environment with Python 3.10–3.11. Configure the metadata and media inputs for a single collection. Keep the optional cloud stages disabled when they are outside the collection’s permissions.

How it uses AI

The editor can turn selected timeline or clip audio into timed subtitles using its Whisper or Vosk engine, then lets the editor correct and export the caption track. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9]

Introduction

Kdenlive keeps a speech-recognition draft in the same timeline where the editor has the source cut. For exhibition and documentary work, this makes it practical to check subtitle timing against the image before sharing an SRT. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9]

What it is good for

Creating a first subtitle pass for a documentary, exhibition recording, tutorial or interview. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9]

The 26.08 manual shows how recognized speech becomes subtitles in the editor. A third-party guide describes the workflow for 26.08.2. A current exact-version independent setup and representative caption comparison remain open. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9]

  2. Compare the editable shape and UVs with the reference and review controls with the next artist.
  3. Inspect material and rig behavior in the intended Blender version before handoff.

Hardware
Minimum system RAM, VRAM and total disk space are not documented in the reviewed instructions.
Software
A compatible agent host and Blender for the editable asset workflow. The separate packaging validator uses Python 3.10+.
Platforms
The source documents a Blender baseline and assistant integration. It does not establish platform-specific editor, renderer or model parity.
